title: GoTrump.com Travel Site Closed About a Year After Its 2006 Launch
description_short: TIME reported that Trump launched the Travelocity-powered GoTrump.com travel search site in 2006 and closed it about a year later.
description_medium: TIME’s 2011 business-failures article says Donald Trump launched GoTrump.com, a luxury travel search engine powered by Travelocity, in 2006 and shut it down about a year later. The source supports the basic launch and closure timeline. It does not provide booking figures, revenue, losses or a stated reason for closing, so the description avoids claims about the venture’s performance or a pattern of failed branding.
description_long: TIME’s article on Donald Trump’s business ventures says he launched GoTrump.com in 2006 as a luxury travel search engine powered by Travelocity and shut the site down about a year later. This supports a straightforward description of the venture’s launch, partner and approximate operating period. The source does not report the site’s number of users, bookings, revenue, costs or financial losses. It also does not establish why the website closed or whether the closure reflected poor performance. The prior description inferred that the site “fizzled” and presented it as evidence of a broader short-lived branding strategy, but those conclusions do not follow from the documented timeline alone. This revised entry preserves the verifiable business event while removing evaluative language that lacks supporting data. The exact source URL in the packet is TIME’s “10 Donald Trump Business Failures” article; its GoTrump section is accessible in the source review. A company filing, archived site announcement or contemporaneous interview would be needed to add a reason for closure or quantify the venture’s commercial results. Until then, the launch and closure dates are the appropriate scope.
notes: The linked TIME page returned HTTP 406 and provided no article text. The populated medium states only that GoTrump.com launched in 2006 with Travelocity and closed about a year later, then adds unsupported judgments about the venture's performance. A readable source account is needed for a useful long explanation; the existing medium is preserved verbatim.
Evidence resolution: revise_narrowly. No financial results, user metrics or closure rationale are provided.

title: Trump’s January 2017 Travel Order Led to Airport Detentions and Court Challenges
description_short: Executive Order 13769 restricted entry from seven countries; airport detentions prompted emergency court orders, and Trump fired Acting Attorney General Sally Yates.
description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 13769 on January 27, 2017, restricting entry from seven predominantly Muslim countries for 90 days and suspending refugee admissions. AP reported airport detentions and a federal judge’s emergency order barring deportation of travelers covered by the ban. DOJ records say Sally Yates directed department lawyers not to defend the order; Trump fired her, and the department later reversed that instruction. These sources support the event without claiming every green-card holder was detained or deported.
description_long: On January 27, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769, which suspended refugee admissions and restricted entry for 90 days for nationals of seven predominantly Muslim countries. The order took effect amid reports of detentions at U.S. airports. The Associated Press reported that a federal judge issued an emergency order temporarily barring deportation of travelers covered by the ban, while the American Civil Liberties Union described specific travelers detained at Logan Airport. Acting Attorney General Sally Yates then instructed Justice Department attorneys not to present arguments defending the order because she was not convinced it was lawful. Trump dismissed Yates, and Deputy Attorney General Dana Boente subsequently directed DOJ to defend the order. These documented events support a concise account of the policy’s immediate airport and legal consequences. The earlier copy used broad language about “chaos,” claimed travelers including green-card holders were detained or deported without specifying cases, and stated the order was quickly blocked by federal injunctions. The revised version grounds those details in dated sources and avoids implying that every affected traveler had the same experience. The later nationwide litigation and subsequent revised order are outside this entry’s narrower scope.

preserved_fields.title: Muslim Ban Executive Order Chaos at Airports
preserved_fields.description_short: Muslim Ban Executive Order Chaos at Airports
preserved_fields.description_medium: On January 27, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769, banning entry to the United States from seven predominantly Muslim countries for 90 days. The sudden implementation sparked widespread chaos and mass protests at major airports as travelers, including green card holders, were detained or deported without warning. Acting Attorney General Sally Yates was fired after instructing the Justice Department not to defend the order in court. The controversial measure drew swift condemnation from civil rights groups and was quickly met with federal injunctions blocking its enforcement.

title: Trump’s 2023 Fauci Accusations Need a Matching Source
description_short: The linked Politico article concerns Robert Redfield’s account of COVID-origin discussions, not the Trump statements named in this title.
description_medium: The linked Politico URL identifies a March 2023 report about former CDC Director Robert Redfield’s account of discussions over COVID-19 origins. It does not substantiate the title’s claims that Trump called Anthony Fauci “Dr. Death,” accused him of funding the virus’s creation, or called for his prosecution. No dated Trump statement or recording supporting those claims is included in the packet. Keep the item unresolved until a matching primary statement or reliable report is supplied.
description_long: The supplied Politico link is a March 8, 2023 article about former CDC Director Robert Redfield’s claim that Anthony Fauci and Francis Collins excluded him from early discussions about COVID-19 origins. That subject is distinct from the title’s assertions about Donald Trump allegedly calling Fauci “Dr. Death,” saying he funded the creation of COVID-19, and seeking his prosecution. The input packet does not include a dated Trump post, speech, recording or contemporaneous report containing those statements. The Politico article therefore cannot serve as evidence for the specific event named in the title, even if it provides separate context about the origins debate. The proposed text makes the citation mismatch explicit and avoids treating the allegation as established fact. The record should remain in needs_context until an editor supplies a source that matches the alleged words and date. If no such source exists, remove the entry or retitle it around Redfield’s account and rewrite it as a separate event using Politico’s reporting. The current record must not combine that report with unsupported accusations. This proposal changes populated title and summary fields transparently and preserves the original source URL for review.

title: Trump Publicly Criticized the Mueller Investigation; Exact Phrase Count Unverified
description_short: Trump publicly criticized the Mueller investigation; the supplied sources do not verify a count of 278 or more uses of “witch hunt.”
description_medium: The Mueller report concerns Russian interference and the investigation into links or coordination with the Trump campaign. It documents the investigation but does not count Trump’s uses of “witch hunt.” The packet provides no dated statement corpus or counting method for the 278-plus figure and no cited passages establishing that the phrase was used to intimidate witnesses or grand jurors. The proposed title keeps the documented criticism and labels the exact count unverified.
description_long: The Justice Department’s 2019 report by Special Counsel Robert Mueller documents the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible links or coordination involving people associated with the Trump campaign. The report is not a dataset counting Donald Trump’s use of the phrase “witch hunt.” The packet contains no dated list of statements, rules for counting repeated or quoted uses, or independent source supporting the title’s total of 278 or more. It also does not identify report passages that establish the asserted purpose of intimidating witnesses or grand jurors. The evidence supports a narrower record about Trump’s public criticism of the investigation, but the exact phrase frequency and claimed intent require separate documentation. This revision removes the numerical claim and avoids presenting motive as fact. The unchanged DOJ source remains useful for the investigation’s scope, while a transparent corpus of dated posts, speeches and interviews would be needed to establish a count. If the collection requires the exact phrase in the title, add a source that documents repeated use and a reproducible method. Do not reinstate the 278-plus figure based solely on the Mueller report.

title: Trump Announced a Planned U.S. Withdrawal from Syria in December 2018
description_short: On December 19, 2018, Trump announced a U.S. withdrawal from Syria and said ISIS had been defeated; he defended the decision publicly the next day.
description_medium: The Washington Post reported that Trump announced on December 19, 2018, that U.S. forces would leave Syria, citing the defeat of ISIS, and quoted his December 20 posts defending the decision. A contemporaneous transcript from his Iraq visit later described a “strong, deliberate, and orderly” withdrawal. The sources support an announced plan, not the unrelated Yahoo page supplied in the record or a claim that a full withdrawal was completed then.
description_long: President Donald Trump announced in December 2018 that U.S. forces would withdraw from Syria, arguing that the Islamic State had been defeated. The Washington Post reported his December 19 announcement and quoted posts he published the next day defending the decision and saying it was time for U.S. forces to come home. A transcript of Trump’s December 26 remarks during a visit to U.S. troops in Iraq described a “strong, deliberate, and orderly withdrawal” while maintaining a U.S. presence in Iraq. Together, these sources document the announcement and how Trump publicly framed it. They do not establish that every U.S. troop left Syria at that time; the administration’s policy and troop levels later changed. The record’s original Yahoo URL now points to an unrelated Netflix story about Squid Game, so it must not be used to support this event. The revised title identifies the announcement date and makes clear that this entry concerns a stated plan. It avoids implying that an announced withdrawal and a completed withdrawal are the same event. Add separate sourcing if this record is meant to cover later implementation or subsequent changes.
notes: Reason: The linked URL now resolves to an unrelated Squid Game story, and the supplied synopsis lacks a date, troop count and scope of the announced withdrawal.
Proposed correction: Replace the link with contemporaneous reporting or an official statement and specify whether the announcement concerned full withdrawal or redeployment.

Evidence resolution: replace_mismatched_source_and_narrow. This does not claim the withdrawal was completed in December 2018. The supplied Yahoo link is unrelated and replaced in the evidence proposal.

title: Trump Granted William E. Henry a Full Pardon on January 19, 2021
description_short: Trump granted William E. “Ed” Henry a full and unconditional pardon for his federal theft-of-government-property conviction on January 19, 2021.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s pardon instrument states that Donald Trump granted William E. Henry, also known as Ed Henry, a full and unconditional pardon on January 19, 2021. It identifies his Middle District of Alabama conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 641 and records a sentence of two years’ probation, a $4,000 fine and a $100 special assessment, imposed May 2, 2019. The instrument does not state the underlying conduct or Trump’s rationale.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted William E. Henry, also known as Ed Henry, a full and unconditional pardon. The Justice Department’s pardon instrument identifies the conviction as a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 641 in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama, docket 2:18cr249-WKW-01. It says Henry was sentenced on May 2, 2019, to two years of probation, a $4,000 fine and a $100 special assessment. The instrument is primary evidence of the pardon and the sentence listed in the grant. It does not describe the underlying conduct, explain why Trump selected Henry for clemency, or establish any improper exchange or corrupt motive. This entry therefore records the documented clemency action without treating the pardon category as proof of corruption. The available DOJ clemency listing and pardon instrument support the date, identity, offense statute and sentence. A case record would be needed to describe the facts of the offense, and a documented statement or contemporaneous record would be needed to attribute a rationale to Trump. The title and short description are narrowed to the official action and avoid unsupported implications.
notes: The linked DOJ listing gives the offense and original sentence but omits the underlying conduct, clemency terms, and documented rationale.
Evidence resolution: revise_to_documented_clemency_facts. The pardon instrument does not describe underlying conduct or rationale. No inference of corrupt motive is supported by this record alone.
